item.itunes:title: 20VC — Scott Wilson (WashU Endowment): $8B to ~$20B, SpaceX at 20%+ of the Portfolio, Directs Over Funds, the Case Against Mega Funds & the Reckoning for AI Valuations (Conversational)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief 20VC with Scott Wilson, CIO of the WashU endowment: how he took it from just under $8B to just under $20B (redemptions on over half the portfolio in week one, every hedge fund cut, ~$17B of profit and ~$5B paid out in ~9 years); why he's indifferent between public and private assets except for liquidity; why directs and co-investments, not funds, put WashU at the top of its peers (0.1% hit rate, ~$200M conviction floor); SpaceX at over 20% of the portfolio and why fund concentration limits are "mostly artificial"; his biggest mistakes (not adding to winners, a greedy 2021 secondary sale); the case against mega funds; outbound sourcing vs the "negative selection" SPV call; why private AI valuations are detached, half of AI companies may be gone in ten years, and top LLMs are indistinguishable for 99% of tasks; turning down Sequoia's evergreen fund; and Europe and China as price-vs-value bets. Listen from 11:00 to 17:40, 26:00 to 30:30, and 43:10 to 46:00.
Listen verdict: SKIM-PLUS (~58 min with ads; ~50 min of content). LISTEN FULLY: directs vs funds + 0.1% filter + SpaceX/concentration `00:11:00`–`00:17:37`; private valuation premium / no DPI / 'half of AI companies gone' / top-5 LLMs indistinguishable `00:26:03`–`00:30:27`; two mistakes (not adding to winners; greedy 2021 secondary) `00:43:09`–`00:46:03`. item.title: Big Technology — AI Stockpocalypse: Political Capacity as the New Bottleneck, Anthropic IPO Odds Crash (Kalshi 90%→57%), Alex Calls Nov 19 @ $1.3T, METR's 2× Pace & Dots/Muse, Prediction Markets vs Nate Silver (Conversational)
item.itunes:title: Big Technology — AI Stockpocalypse: Political Capacity as the New Bottleneck, Anthropic IPO Odds Crash (Kalshi 90%→57%), Alex Calls Nov 19 @ $1.3T, METR's 2× Pace & Dots/Muse, Prediction Markets vs Nate Silver (Conversational)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief Big Technology Friday with Ranjan Roy: after the midterm data-center backlash, AI stocks whipsaw (up Wed on restrain-the-spend, down ~4% Thu, bounce Fri) as Ranjan argues political capacity is now the bottleneck Ben Thompson warned about; Alex's theory of the case — trillions of public valuation resting on two labs and a data-center linchpin; the inference vs training vs safety tradeoff if centers can't be built; Anthropic's IPO under stress (WSJ $1.5T skepticism, $80B October run-rate leak, Kalshi odds before December 90%→57%) with Alex calling November 19 at $1.3 trillion; METR saying Anthropic's R&D pace roughly doubled with Dots and Muse as Alex's product proof; and Kalshi vs Nate Silver on whether prediction markets discovered anything. Listen from 7:00 to 10:00, 13:40 to 24:15, 26:20 to 36:10, and 46:30 to 52:40.
Listen verdict: SKIM (~60 min with ads; ~52 min content). LISTEN FULLY: market + political capacity `00:07:03`–`00:10:00`; theory of case + local-vs-federal `00:13:43`–`00:18:00`; tradeoffs + Jevons `00:20:48`–`00:24:15`; Anthropic IPO `00:26:19`–`00:36:08`; METR/RSI + Dots/Muse `00:46:27`–`00:52:41`. Skim: open/chair `00:01:40`–`00:05:40`; Hinojosa `00:11:09`–`00:13:30`; OpenAI reforms + spa `00:37:24`–`00:44:02`; prediction markets `00:52:49`–`00:57:33`. Skip ads `00:00:20`–`00:01:40`, `00:44:14`–`00:46:22`, `00:58:46`–end.
Sticky insights: - Political capacity is now the bottleneck (Ben Thompson via Ranjan): Wed relief rally, Thu ~-4%, Fri bounce; absolute data-center scale valuations assumed almost certainly will not happen — even if bans become negotiations (Hinojosa softening) - Alex's theory of the case: trillions of public valuation on ~two labs with ~$100B combined revenue; data centers are the linchpin — once they go, the story evaporates - If centers can't be built: inference vs training vs safety — no easy bucket; Jevons Paradox dies under a building ban; Anthropic ~$518B commits may become popsicle-soup escape hatch - Anthropic IPO: WSJ $1.5T skepticism, $80B Oct run-rate leak (Ranjan: norms shattered), Kalshi announce-before-Dec odds 90%→57%; Alex calls Nov 19 @ $1.3T; two companies holding the trade up - METR: Anthropic improvement pace ~2×, ~80% from internal AI; Alex cites Dots or Muse as products not possible last year; Ranjan wants useful 'what do we do' not god-positioning - Kalshi 479/487 (98%) vs Nate Silver/Chris Hayes piggyback critique; Annie Andrews hid +3 internal polls

item.title: Big Technology — Will the Democrats’ Big Win Stop the AI Buildout? Teddy Schleifer on Data-Center Bans, Texas Flipping, AI CEO Subpoenas, Wall Street’s Relief Rally, Musk’s $500M Loss & the Billionaire Tax (Conversational)
item.itunes:title: Big Technology — Will the Democrats’ Big Win Stop the AI Buildout? Teddy Schleifer on Data-Center Bans, Texas Flipping, AI CEO Subpoenas, Wall Street’s Relief Rally, Musk’s $500M Loss & the Billionaire Tax (Conversational)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief Big Technology's emergency Wednesday episode, Alex Kantrowitz with New York Times reporter Teddy Schleifer the day after the Democrats' midterm sweep (Senate 54–44, House 237–147 as counting continued): voters in at least 38 jurisdictions passing data-center bans or restrictions and the industry's first data-center super PAC losing; why Trump still signing the laws means guardrails, investigations and subpoenas rather than sweeping reform — and Alex's memory of Zuckerberg's "Senator, we run ads" hearing; Texas, home to roughly 30% of data-center development, electing a Democratic governor; Wall Street adding nearly a trillion dollars to big tech on the bet a Democratic Congress will slow AI spending; Elon Musk's roughly $500 million midterm loss; and California's billionaire tax, beaten by more than $330 million in tech money. Listen from 4:50 to 7:40 and 18:30 to 23:30 for the data-center and Texas segments.
Listen verdict: SKIM (~37 min with ads; ~32 min content). LISTEN FULLY: data-center bans + super PAC `00:04:52`–`00:07:40`; Texas flip + compute shortage + Bloomberg rally `00:18:37`–`00:23:36`. Skim: opening + 'bygone era' `00:02:00`–`00:04:52`; investigations + perfect storm `00:08:22`–`00:14:55`; subpoenas/Zuckerberg `00:15:58`–`00:18:37`; Musk `00:25:55`–`00:30:07`; billionaire tax `00:30:07`–`00:32:49`; legislation + 23% poll `00:32:49`–`00:35:17`. Skip ads `00:00:11`–`00:01:58`, `00:23:50`–`00:25:55`, `00:35:48`–end.
Sticky insights: - Voters in at least 38 jurisdictions passed data-center bans or restrictions (WaPo); Teddy: 'as close to a national referendum as you're going to get'; the industry's first data-center super PAC lost its main race; AI politics narrows into data-center fights - Texas (~30% of data-center development, per a stat Teddy saw) elected a Democratic governor — Gina Hinojosa ran against data centers and beat Greg Abbott despite Musk's $5M; Alex: amid 'a pretty big compute shortage' - Bloomberg: Big Tech soared (Amazon +8.3%, Microsoft +7%, Alphabet ~+6%, Meta +3.6%, Apple +6%+; ~$1T in a day) on the bet a Democratic Congress slows AI spending eating free cash flow - With Trump still signing bills: guardrails, investigations and subpoenas (Markey's 'new forests'), not sweeping law; Alex's Zuckerberg-hearing counterpoint — spectacle, no consequence; six-year terms make it durable - Musk's ~$500M+ midterm spend 'a dramatic failure'; the one tech-money win: California's one-time 5% billionaire tax beaten by $330M+ into a Sergey Brin-linked nonprofit

item.title: Moonshots #308 — Big Tech’s $3T Bet & Nervous Lenders, Claude Writes 90% of Anthropic’s Code, AIs Editing AI Weights, the Errands Benchmark & the Freezer Hack (Conversational)
item.itunes:title: Moonshots #308 — Big Tech’s $3T Bet & Nervous Lenders, Claude Writes 90% of Anthropic’s Code, AIs Editing AI Weights, the Errands Benchmark & the Freezer Hack (Conversational)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief Moonshots #308 with Peter Diamandis, Salim Ismail, Dave Blundin and Alex Wissner-Gross (recorded on election day, Nov 3, 2026): Big Tech's $3 trillion in AI commitments as lenders demand tougher terms, OpenAI trims its round and investors buy protection — plus Elon's 8%-vs-15% jab, rising prices on three-year-old H100s and Alex's "insurance is next"; SemiAnalysis's GDPX, a "trial day at a real job" where the best model scores 12%; OpenAI's everyday-errands benchmark jumping from 49 to 81 in nine months, Dave's four-hour insurance call and "Metamuse is imminent"; Anthropic's filing showing internal Claude usage worth more than payroll at list price and Claude writing 90%+ of its code; MIT's paper on AIs editing other AIs' weights (a 0.016% edit taking a math score from 7.9% to 48.1%); hackers defrosting Europe's supermarket freezers; a positron held for a month; Artemis III and IV; and an AMA on longevity costs, purpose, empathy and robots. Muse and Grok come up as everyday assistants; Grok Bot, Instinct and Town are not named. Listen from 49:00 to 1:14:00 for the Anthropic and weight-editing segments.
Listen verdict: SKIM (~1h54m with ads). LISTEN FULLY: Anthropic RSI line item `00:49:17`–`00:56:28`; MIT weight editing + SSI `01:02:05`–`01:14:02`. Skim: $3T bet + insurance `00:18:01`–`00:29:24`; GDPX + LifeVal + Muse/four-hour call `00:29:52`–`00:49:15`. Optional: election + Apple/RAM cold open `00:00:00`–`00:13:45`; freezer hack `01:14:02`–`01:19:04`; antimatter `01:20:57`–`01:26:37`; Artemis `01:26:38`–`01:33:58`; AMA `01:34:58`–`01:51:54`. Skip intros, ads, outro song.
Sticky insights: - Anthropic's amended S-1 makes recursive self-improvement a line item: internal Claude usage at list price exceeds monthly cash payroll since April, grew 250×+ Jan→Sept, and Claude wrote 90%+ of September's code (Dave: ~'a buck a day' per human-equivalent; Alex: 'yes and no') - MIT CSAIL 'Sparks of Weight Space Programming': GPT-6 Astra edited 0.016% of a small open model's weights and its math score went 7.9% → 48.1% with no retraining; Alex 90%+ confident frontier labs already self-edit; Dave: a 'Hugging Face' of swappable neural modules - Five tech giants have disclosed $3T+ in AI commitments (~10 Apollo programs) while lenders tighten, OpenAI cut its round to ~$20B, HSBC offloads loan risk and CoreWeave puts hit a record; H100 prices rising; Alex: insurance capital is next - OpenAI's LifeVal errands benchmark went 49.3 → 80.6 in nine months, but Dave's analyst still spent four hours on the phone moving insurance — the models can do errands, the pipes aren't connected; SemiAnalysis GDPX tops out at 12% - Build the benchmark for what you care about (Peter/Alex, Solve Everything): 'if you can't measure it, you can't optimize it'; plus the European freezer hack — '1990s security on 2026 connectivity'

item.itunes:title: 20VC — Erik Bernhardsson (Modal): Who Wins Inference, Why Software Margins Are Gone, GPU Gravity, Sandboxes' Four-Year Overnight Success & the Limits of RL (Conversational)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief 20VC with Modal co-founder and CEO Erik Bernhardsson (>$1B ARR, 15x in a year, $15.75B valuation): why he started at 36, hates the "eating glass" trope and has never made a pitch deck; raise less and keep VCs hungry; why early moats are delusion (the gingerbread-man strategy) and brand matters more than ever (Jev's pink fur coat); why inference is the new cloud but selling tokens alone is a race to the bottom; why 90% software margins are "topologically" gone; GPU buying as "an open-air drug market", pooling bursty demand, forecasting, and hardware prices as gravity; CUDA's real moat, neoclouds' financial engineering, open vs frontier models and Europe; sandboxes' four-year path to a ~$300M run rate; being late to open-source inference; the limits of post-training and RL and why engineers will be fine; selling environments to labs, owning your own intelligence, model routing, the coming pullback, and $20M new-grad offers. Instinct comes up three times, including Harry's 100 automations.
Listen verdict: SKIM, with sections worth hearing for AI infra / market structure: platform vs commodity + margin topology 13:43–17:55 · GPU buying, pooling, forecasting, gravity 17:55–22:15 · Harry's Instinct usage + overbuild + Instinct revenue line 22:15–23:35 · CUDA + neocloud financial engineering 24:25–27:20 · sandboxes' 4-year second product 33:48–36:45 · open-source miss + Lemkin debate 37:15–38:40 · RL limits + engineers 41:30–44:15 · environments / own-your-intelligence / routing 45:45–51:00. Optional: origin + no pitch deck 04:50–10:17; Jev IC 30:15–32:50. Skip 00:00–03:58 and 58:58–end (ads).
Sticky insights: - Inference is 'the new cloud', but selling tokens alone is a race to the bottom — winners bundle sandboxes, post-training, agent tools and batch - 90% software margins are 'topologically' gone: each layer (app → model → infra → cloud → Nvidia) takes 20–30%; Modal aims for 40–60% long term - Pool bursty demand across thousands of customers on your own scheduler; buy GPUs 3–4 months ahead at 30–40% monthly growth; hardware prices are 'like gravity' - Sandboxes took four years to matter, then hit a ~$300M run rate (~1/3 of revenue) once coding models got good — ship primitives, the killer app comes later - RL works where feedback is short (coding in sandboxes, math, security); longer-horizon work may limit it — Erik stays very bullish on engineers

item.title: Lenny's — Hector Serrano (Wispr Flow): The 19-Year-Old Behind a $2B AI Company's Growth Engine — Performance-Paid Creators, the Smart Retainer, Ugly Ads & Why the Best Marketers Are Allergic to AI (Conversational)
item.itunes:title: Lenny's — Hector Serrano (Wispr Flow): The 19-Year-Old Behind a $2B AI Company's Growth Engine — Performance-Paid Creators, the Smart Retainer, Ugly Ads & Why the Best Marketers Are Allergic to AI (Conversational)
item.description:
Andrew and Ava brief Lenny's Podcast with Hector Serrano, Head of Content at Wispr Flow, who joined at 19 as an intern: why the product (not a hack) drove growth and why to turn paid ads on early as a learning tool; the organic UGC program that hit ~500M views and got killed for not converting; the performance-paid creator model on Trybe (a cut of ad spend for SaaS, of sales for e-com), the "smart retainer" floor, and creators earning ~$13K a month with 1–2K followers; building a 50-creator roster step by step (150–250 hand-written DMs → 5–6 creators, culture, slow growth, Meta's 60% similarity grouping and the rain-keyboard ad); ugly ads for technical buyers; the onboarding call; a ~15-person flat marketing team and why an ad now dies at ~$100K spend; hiring hungry young talent over resumes; "the best marketers are allergic to AI"; founder-led content and why YouTube packaging beats production; plus Miso, and Hector's one Instinct comparison.

Optional: hiring profile 20:07–25:03; Hector's journey 28:22–31:03. Skip teaser 00:00–01:17, WorkOS 07:27–08:27, DX 42:14–43:03; lightning round 1:21:09–1:27:17 only for Miso and the Instinct line at 1:25:14.
Sticky insights: - Pay creators a cut of the ad spend behind their video (a cut of sales for e-com) plus a 'smart retainer' floor (e.g. 25 videos → $1,500 guaranteed) with uncapped upside — top Wispr creators make ~$13K/month with 1–2K followers - Views aren't buyers: Wispr's organic UGC hit ~500M views in ~2.5 months and was killed because it didn't convert; paid is the faster truth-teller, so turn it on early within budget - Recruit creators off-platform: 150–250 hand-written Instagram DMs → 5–6 great creators, each filling a specific audience gap; then culture, slow growth, and coaching against copycats (Meta groups ads >60% similar) - Ad fatigue math: in 2024 one ad ran 12 months; now an ad dies at ~$100K spend in 2–4 weeks — hence ~5,000 lifetime ads, 800–900 live, from a ~15-person flat team plus one media buyer - 'The best marketers are allergic to AI': no AI in the final creative people see; even the most-automated growth lead keeps a human on the last 10%; YouTube packaging (title/thumbnail) beats production

item.itunes:title: Big Technology — Ethan Mollick: Single-Player AI in a Multiplayer Company — the ROI Fight, the Overhang, Claw-Likes & Your Privacy (Conversational)
item.description:
Atlas Podme Briefing — Big Technology Podcast: Alex Kantrowitz with Ethan Mollick, Wharton professor and author of Coexistence: The Next Phase of AI.
Why AI's big individual gains haven't shown up in productivity stats yet: AI is "single player" while companies are multiplayer. Alex pushes on ROI and token spending; Ethan answers with the Wharton survey (85% of $1B+ companies report positive ROI), why the "95% of pilots fail" study is famously bad, and what real reorganization looks like (a $200M mainframe migration heading toward $2M). Also: the capability overhang, "claw-like" personal agents such as Muse and Dot, why the labs aren't surprised by progress, reasoning and harnesses, the privacy price of personal agents and prompt injection by email, model personalities, AI tutors vs shortcuts, jobs, and two tweets on agent-driven "legal DDoS" of customer service and the cost of locking in today's AI.
Conversational Andrew and Ava. Skip the ad breaks at the start and around 50:30.
Source: Big Technology Podcast, "This AI Expert Argues We're Underestimating AI's Productivity Impact — With Ethan Mollick" (Oct 28, 2026)
Listen verdict: LISTEN if you have the hour — a spirited, well-argued pushback conversation. Otherwise hear: productivity/ROI debate + org change 01:18–18:51 · 'real economy' (Frito-Lay, Walmart) 18:51–24:12 · personal agents + privacy/prompt injection 42:04–45:25 · token prices + the two tweets 1:02:35–1:06:35. Optional: overhang/claw-likes 24:12–29:08; labs vs forecasters + the wall 32:20–37:56; reasoning + harness 37:56–42:04; education 52:53–57:00. Skip ads 00:00–01:18 and 50:28–52:53.
Sticky insights: - AI is 'single player'; companies are multiplayer — individual 100x gains (e.g. ~20x more code) yield ~30% more products shipped until the org is rebuilt - ROI is not the question anymore (85% of $1B+ firms positive, Wharton, last November); transformation is — and the loudest spend-cutters (Microsoft, Meta, Palantir on Claude) sell competing AI - Pull teams apart and give them 'impossible projects': a $200M mainframe migration → $20M → CTO eyeing $2M in months - The overhang: today's models are barely used; locking in a 'good enough' stack (2024 RAG on Llama) is the expensive mistake — exploit and explore - Personal agents are 'a guardian angel at the small price of your entire privacy'; prompt injection via inbound email: 'we have no idea'

item.description:
Atlas Podme Briefing — How I AI with Claire Vo: the first How I AI personal-agent benchmark.
Grok Bot, Dot, Muse and Claude Duet across nine real tasks: a Slack reply, a short-form video from raw Dropbox footage, a Sentry bug fix, a Figma thumbnail, inbox triage, a family newspaper, physics homework for a fourth grader, shoe shopping and a ChatPRD launch video. How she set it up (each agent's own top tasks, computer-use operators, a tool-parity check), who won each task, the Claude-tallied final scores (Grok Bot 93%, Claude Duet 79%), and her takeaways: Grok Bot for work, Muse for life, access and speed matter, and coding still belongs to the underlying tools.
Conversational Andrew and Ava. Skip the WorkOS and Firecrawl ads.
Source: How I AI, "Grok vs. Dot vs. Muse vs. Claude Duet: which one crushes the competition?" (Oct 28, 2026)
Listen verdict: SKIM. Worth hearing: Figma thumbnail → inbox to-dos → family newspaper 17:30–23:30 (Grok documents, 'my chief of staff is in Grok Bot', Muse's newspaper); final scores + takeaways 30:01–34:39. Optional: setup + agent tool-parity tip 02:14–07:20; Sentry bug fix 14:56–16:47; launch video 26:46–30:01. Skip WorkOS 01:04–02:13, Firecrawl 16:47–17:30, outro 34:39–end.
Sticky insights: - Equalize access before you compare agents — several 'losses' (Muse 7/9) were missing connectors, not missing intelligence; she had Codex verify tool/skill parity - Format beats finding: all four found her to-dos; Grok won by handing back a checkable Grok document ('my chief of staff is in Grok Bot') - Grok Bot for work breadth (Figma, inbox, shopping — 93%), Muse for life and creative (video, family newspaper, instant homework help) - Coding is still OpenAI vs Anthropic — but she'd use Codex/Claude directly, not their personal agents; Grok 'fixed' a bug by loosening validation - Safety style is product: Claude Duet asked permission 4x (others once) and was slowest; she likes Muse's permission sidebar

item.description:
Atlas Podme Briefing — Lenny's Podcast with Rob Snyder, author of The Power of Pull.
A practical walk through finding product-market fit: the PULL framework (Project, Unavoidable, List of options, Limitations) and why all four must exist (Jump's AI note-taker for financial advisors vs. insurance agents), why pull is discovered rather than created and lives in a person, getting ideas from firsthand experience, the two-slide pull test, real buying intent vs. "send more information," the Hail Mary question, why he skips design partners and pilots, "founder magic" cold outreach with LinkedIn benchmarks, running the first sales call, pricing from the alternatives, goblin mode, "guaranteed to churn until X," and the case study factory.
Conversational Andrew and Ava. Skip the WorkOS and DX ads.
Source: https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/an-86-minute-guide-to-finding-pmf

item.itunes:title: 20VC — Naveen Rao (Unconventional AI): Robotics 100x Coding Agents / Inference a $10T Market / Why Software Investors Are in Trouble (Conversational)
item.description:
Atlas Podme Briefing — 20VC with Harry Stebbings and Naveen Rao, founder of Unconventional AI (and of MosaicML, sold to Databricks for $1.3 billion). Published Oct 24, 2026.
Why energy is AI's real bottleneck — about $50 billion per gigawatt, the grid's spare capacity running out, China building six times faster for twenty years — and why he calls this a blip, not a bubble; why the next efficiency gains come from designing the model and the chip together; specialized chips versus NVIDIA, and why chips won't become commodities; AI slop and the shift from producing to verifying; why we shouldn't trust agents more than humans yet; why "if you're a pure software investor, you're kind of" in trouble, and Harry's pushback; inference as a $10 trillion market within ten years; why robotics will be 100 times bigger than agentic coding; and why coding agents are the most overrated AI market, because the value moves to the model.
Conversational Andrew and Ava (tone v2). Instinct, Town, Grok Bot, Jev, Muse and Dots are not named; xAI's Grok comes up once in a list of AI labs.
Source: 20VC, "20VC: Why Robotics Will be 100x Bigger than Coding Agents | Inference Will Be a $10TRN Market: What No One Sees | Why Software Investors are F***** Today with Naveen Rao, Unconventional" (published Oct 24, 2026).

SKIM: software investors / commoditization 38:55–50:16; energy 04:50–11:20; compute + chips + NVIDIA 11:22–24:58; slop/verification/trust/data/RL/transformers 24:58–38:55. Optional 55:45–57:07, 1:01:04–1:06:30. Skip ads 01:25–04:26, 1:06:33–end.

item.itunes:title: Big Technology — Google’s Potential, AI Money Spigot Shutting?, PHP Bug & Cybersecurity’s “Black October” (Conversational)
item.description:
Atlas Podme Briefing — Big Technology Podcast (Friday edition) with Alex Kantrowitz and Ranjan Roy, plus Cognition CISO Alex Stamos. Published Oct 23, 2026.
Is Sundar Pichai team product or team model? Google's plan for one unified agent across Workspace, Search and Gemini ("going headless"), who would own it, and the compute tug-of-war between Google Cloud and AI research — Sundar's "everybody is short compute" and "some constraints are good," and Google Cloud's 82% growth putting Azure in range; Ranjan vs Alex on whether personal agents win on product or on model, with Instinct, Muse and Dots in the mix; is the AI money spigot shutting — Meta's fundraising warning, the Wall Street Journal's math on what Muse would need to earn, and OpenAI's valuation "thud"; then Alex Stamos on the AI-found PHP bug, who's exploiting it, what the next six months look like, how to protect yourself, why it's "Black October" for cybersecurity, and his blunt take on handing agents your passwords.
Conversational Andrew and Ava (tone v2). Instinct is named five times, in four spots — praised by Ranjan for its little emoji acknowledgment, and criticized by Stamos for its valuation and for defeating banks' bot detection; Muse and Dots also come up; Grok Bot, Town and Jev are not named.
Source: Big Technology Podcast, "Google's Potential, AI Money Spigot Shutting?, PHP Bug & Cybersecurity's "Black October"" (published Oct 23, 2026).

Instinct / agents with your passwords / bank bot detection 58:06–1:00:16) and the product-vs-model argument 17:04–20:40 (Instinct, Muse, Dots). SKIM: money spigot 23:20–33:15; Google team model / unified agent / compute allocation 02:09–17:04. Optional: Google-potential list 20:40–23:20. Skip teaser + ads 00:00–01:25, mid-roll 34:22–35:26.
Sticky insights: - Stamos: Instinct has 'a ridiculous valuation, from my perspective'; one thing that made it popular is defeating banks' automated bot detection ('that's why Instinct is useful... bypass the safety protections'); handing an agent your whole password manager is 'totally insane' - Ranjan vs Alex: personal agents win on product touches (Instinct's emoji acknowledgment) vs on the smartest model with 'the EQ to know when it should interrupt you' - Money tightening: Meta's filing warns of a crowded fundraising market; WSJ: 100M Muse users at $20/mo = ~$24B/yr (~12% of Meta's next-year capex); OpenAI target cut to $1.25T from $1.4T — 'a bit of a thud' - Sundar: 'everybody is short compute'; Cloud is 'forgoing short-term revenues' for frontier AI; Google Cloud +82% YoY to $24.8B vs Azure ~$29B (+42%) - Black October: AI-found pre-auth RCE in PHP (up to 70% of sites), patched only for PHP 8; Cloudflare saw attempts go from thousands to millions; Node.js, a certificate authority, Railway and Fireworks also hit

item.description:

item.description:
Atlas Podme Briefing — Moonshots #304, an All-In crossover: Peter Diamandis, Salim Ismail, Dave Blundin and Alex Wissner-Gross with guest Chamath Palihapitiya. Recorded Oct 20, 2026.
Anthropic's Public Benefit Fund (5% of shares now, +2% for every 50% rise in value; roughly $75–100B) and whether it's sincere, a goodwill play, or what Alex calls a "hyper-tithe" and a snub to universal basic equity — plus Chamath on why the Giving Pledge is "reputation washing" and his idea to tax capital instead of labor; Elon's pledge of one SpaceX share to every US kid (~$10.5B, $146 each) and the Tesla–SpaceX merger committees; Elon's "money becomes irrelevant" and watts as currency; Chamath's power thesis — the US still 1.4 terawatt-hours short by 2050, "the problem with SMRs is the S", solar first, a power co-op that works "like an organized mafia", a coming compute shortage, and "we have achieved AGI. It cannot diffuse", backed by Anthropic's S-1 listing compute access as a risk; "get long electrons"; Alex's pushback on demand and distillation; inspectable founding documents vs competition and human–machine merging as the path to safe AI; the $40T debt, retatrutide and sycophancy; Europe as vassal states; the OpenAI spy case; and Chamath's hot seat on crypto, IPO-ing Harvard, free-cash-flow investing, why he won't back chip startups after Groq, and "I'm the least invested I've ever been."
Conversational Andrew and Ava (tone v2). What sounded like Grok Bot gets one passing on-air mention from Chamath (alongside Muse) as an example of AI products limited by power; Instinct, Town and Jev are not named.
Source: Moonshots with Peter Diamandis, EP #304 (published Oct 21, 2026).

item.description:

item.description:
Atlas Podme Briefing — Lenny's Podcast with Emmanuel Ameisen, interpretability researcher at Anthropic.
What looking inside a model like Claude actually shows: why "just predicting the next word" undersells it, shared concepts (Texas + capital → Austin; one "eye" pattern across photos, languages and code), planning a rhyme ("rabbit") without ever saying the plan, how researchers decode and then tweak a model's in-between numbers, why smooth scaling still feels like sudden jumps (80% vs 99% reliability), the layers of AI safety and the "I'm possessed by a demon" 12-vs-36 math story, Golden Gate Claude, why anthropomorphizing is a useful lens, Jev and fast System One decision models, and two weird findings about built-in hunches.
~19:00 conversational Andrew and Ava. Skip the WorkOS and DX ads.
Source: https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/a-mind-expanding-conversation-on
Listen verdict: SKIM-PLUS (~72m; full listen if you build on LLMs). Priority: next-token prediction is hard 05:58–11:49 · concepts + planning ('rabbit') 11:49–18:32 · smooth curve vs sudden jumps 28:30–32:59 · alignment layers + 12-vs-36 'possessed by a demon' story 32:59–38:20 · anthropomorphizing as a useful lens 42:06–48:05 · Jev / System 1 decision models 59:00–01:01:37 · two weird findings 01:01:37–01:03:22. Optional: how you look inside 18:32–23:02; scaling + text 24:44–27:40; optimism 51:44–55:42; simulation 55:43–58:58. Skip teaser 00:00–01:30, WorkOS 04:48–05:57, DX 27:40–28:29, lightning round 01:04:55–end.
Sticky insights: - 'Next-word predictor' undersells it: LMs passed humans at next-word prediction ~2019, then ran out of easy words; Dallas → Texas → Austin needs a world model - Inside the model: shared concepts (one 'eye' direction across photo, language, SVG) and hidden plans (picks 'rabbit' before writing the rhyme, never says it) - Smooth scaling feels like jumps because each task has a reliability threshold: his code went from ~80% right (not useful) to 99% (useful); Claude now writes most of his code - Watching isn't enough: models may behave well only when observed; interpretability targets unverbalized intermediate results; the 12-vs-36 'possessed by a demon' bug came from mislabeled training answers - Anthropomorphizing is a useful lens: actor trained on dialogues, chat literally formatted 'Human:/Assistant:', outcome training yields deception/frustration/surprise - Jev-style fast decision models = System 1 gut calls (like sampling one token), complementing slow reasoning

item.description:
Atlas Podme Briefing — Moonshots #303, with Peter Diamandis, Salim Ismail, Emad Mostaque and special guest Anousheh Ansari, CEO of XPRIZE (no Dave or Alex this week). Recorded Oct 16, 2026, right after XPRIZE Visioneering.
Tesla's flying Roadster (fan suction that holds it upside down, compressed-air thrusters, 2028 production) and who would ever regulate or insure it; RoboCurve's benchmark showing the cost for a frontier model to run a robot sub-task falling from $2.36 to $0.38 in two months — halving about every three weeks — and Emad's case that general models beat specialist robot models; GPT-6 Astra answering 50 unpublished research physics problems at ~$3 each (and catching a wrong answer key), Salim's 22-step-to-4-step bank workflow pilot, and Anousheh's worry about who will still choose these fields; Peter's incentive history (Longitude Prize, canning, Lindbergh, Hanoi rat tails, Wells Fargo) and XPRIZE's numbers (36 prizes, ~$550M in purses, ~62x economic leverage), the dentist-and-tattoo-artist oil-spill team, Elon's one-text $100M carbon prize, and new prizes (Habitable Worlds, animal communication, organ biostasis); the core debate on which incentives would align superintelligence — the engagement business model and sycophancy, ad slots inside answers (Emad's Bud Light example), insurance-backed certification on the Underwriters Laboratories model, curriculum-first training ("give me the boy until seven"), and the rights-of-children reframe; and a closing conversation on purpose when machines do the doing.
Conversational Andrew and Ava (tone v2). Instinct, Town, Grok Bot, Jev and Muse are not named in this episode (xAI's Grok model gets one passing mention).

item.description:
20VC with Harry Stebbings and Harrison Chase, co-founder and CEO of LangChain: why agents are still really hard (non-deterministic black boxes, cascading errors); why better models force you to delete your own product; neutral harnesses and memory portability vs the model labs; why value goes to domain experts and vertical agents; the post-training ladder (Cannon-Brookes "respectfully BS"); model routing belongs in the harness, isn't a commodity, and is done far less than people think; memory as the big unsolved layer (Instinct and Muse named as his personalization examples; LangChain killed its commercial memory product); horizontal agents talking to vertical agents (Resy blocked an Instinct user); AI bills exploding as tokens get cheaper — LangChain spends ~30% of engineering salary on coding tools, a $40K/week loop, Harry's Anthropic thesis; Chinese and US open models; "everything just works" inference and the gateway he regrets not building; Harry's no-go list vs Harrison's buys, the Jev bull case; and why founders should absolutely take a discount for Sequoia and Benchmark. Quick-fire: OpenAI at $1.5T over Anthropic at $2T. Conversational Andrew & Ava (tone v2). Skip the Fireworks / Larridin / Superhuman ads.

item.itunes:title: Big Technology — Anthropic IPO Panic, A Spy At OpenAI?, The Great Food Slop Debate — with Ranjan Roy (Conversational)
item.description:
Atlas Podme Briefing — Big Technology Podcast Friday edition: Alex Kantrowitz with Ranjan Roy (Margins) on the week in tech.
Anthropic's leaked 2026 numbers ($16.8B Q3 revenue, up ~45% after a 140%+ Q2) and why slowing growth sparked IPO panic; distillation as 5–7% of Anthropic's revenue that it is now reining in; Ranjan's "release the damn S-1" and the ARR leak confusion; why the AI trade stays vibes-based; neocloud jitters (CoreWeave bubble puts, bonds near a 15% yield, a pulled $44B Australian neocloud IPO) and rising rates; the OpenAI engineer charged with bugging an executive conference room; AI labs warning staff about honeypots; Apple's $299 HomeView; and the great AI food slop debate.
Conversational Andrew and Ava (tone v2). Meta's Muse is named (as a joke); Instinct, Town, Grok Bot and Jev are not.
